title: Skin Layers, Junctions, Dermis, and Adnexa
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter builds the skin from the surface down: the epidermal layers and the keratinocytes that mature through them, the resident melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells, the junctions that hold keratinocytes to each other and to the basement membrane, the dermis and hypodermis, and the glands, hair, and nails. Board questions on skin usually describe a blister, a biopsy report, or a pattern of sweating or hair loss and ask which structure or protein has failed. If you know which protein holds each level together and what happens when it fails, you can predict the split level, the type of blister, how it heals, and the histologic term a pathologist would use.
prerequisites: Epithelial tissue classification and the general structure of cell junctions
Intermediate filaments, actin, and the cadherin and integrin adhesion families
Collagen types I, III, IV, and VII and where each is found
Sympathetic transmitters and receptors, including the cholinergic sympathetic exception
Type II and type IV hypersensitivity and complement activation

connections.how: Langerhans cells start the sensitization phase of allergic contact dermatitis, and pemphigus and pemphigoid are antibody-mediated (type II) injuries to adhesion proteins.
Meissner, Pacinian, and Merkel endings feed large myelinated afferents into the dorsal column pathway, while free nerve endings feed the spinothalamic pathway.
Melanin is made from tyrosine by tyrosinase, and mutations in keratins, laminin 332, and collagens XVII and VII cause the inherited epidermolysis bullosa groups.
Androgens drive sebaceous gland growth and the miniaturization of scalp follicles, and puberty activates apocrine glands.
Defective CFTR in the eccrine sweat duct produces the high sweat chloride used to diagnose cystic fibrosis.

A spot junction that joins two cells through desmoglein and desmocollin cadherins and anchors keratin filaments on each side.
A junction on the basal surface of basal keratinocytes that attaches their keratin filaments to the basement membrane.
The layered junction between epidermis and dermis: lamina lucida, lamina densa, and sublamina densa anchoring fibrils.

Loss of cohesion between keratinocytes, so that they separate and round up within the epidermis.
Separation of the epidermis when apparently normal skin is rubbed sideways, seen when the split is within the epidermis.
Secretion in which the whole cell fills with product and breaks down to release it, as in sebaceous glands.
A hair follicle with its sebaceous gland and arrector pili muscle, the unit involved in acne.
The region of the outer root sheath at the arrector pili insertion that holds the follicle's stem cells.

blocks.text: The epidermis is a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with no blood vessels; it is fed by diffusion from capillary loops in the dermal papillae. Most of its cells are keratinocytes, which are born in the deepest layer and pushed toward the surface. Each layer is therefore one stage in the life of the same cell, and its name describes how that stage looks under the microscope.

The stratum basale is a single row of dividing stem and transit-amplifying cells on the basement membrane. They make keratins 5 and 14, a type II and type I pair that forms a flexible filament network anchored to hemidesmosomes below and desmosomes at the sides. As daughter cells enter the stratum spinosum they switch to keratins 1 and 10 and build thicker filament bundles that insert into many desmosomes. When cells shrink during tissue processing these junctions stretch into the short projections that give the layer its name.

In the stratum granulosum the cells assemble the barrier. Basophilic keratohyalin granules hold profilaggrin and loricrin; profilaggrin is cleaved to filaggrin, which packs keratin filaments into dense bundles, and its breakdown products help the corneum hold water. Lamellar bodies discharge lipid between the cells, where enzymes convert it to ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids that form sheets blocking water loss. Transglutaminase cross-links involucrin, loricrin, and other proteins beneath the plasma membrane into the cornified envelope, and the cell then destroys its nucleus and organelles in a specialized form of programmed death.

The stratum corneum is made of flat, anucleate corneocytes set in lipid, often described as bricks and mortar. Proteases slowly digest the remaining desmosomes so single cells shed from the surface, and the trip from basal layer to shedding takes about 4 weeks. Thick skin of the palms and soles adds a thin, pale-staining stratum lucidum between the granulosum and corneum, has a far thicker corneum, and lacks hair follicles.

blocks.caption: Surface to deep, the order is corneum, lucidum (thick skin only), granulosum, spinosum, basale.

blocks.title: Keratinocyte maturation, basale to corneum
steps: Basal stem cell divides, expressing keratins 5 and 14
Daughter cell enters spinosum and switches to keratins 1 and 10

blocks.caption: The whole journey takes about 4 weeks in normal skin and only a few days in psoriasis.

blocks.text: A defect at each stage produces a distinct disease. Keratin 5 or 14 mutations make basal cells fragile (epidermolysis bullosa simplex, C04), and keratin 1 or 10 mutations make suprabasal cells fragile (epidermolytic ichthyosis). Loss-of-function filaggrin mutations weaken the barrier, causing ichthyosis vulgaris and raising the risk of atopic dermatitis. In psoriasis, transit shortens so much that cells reach the surface with nuclei still present (C08).

blocks.predict: If lamellar bodies could not deliver their lipids but keratin and the cornified envelope formed normally, how would the skin behave?
blocks.explain: Corneocytes would form, but without lipid sheets between them water would leak out freely. Transepidermal water loss rises and the skin becomes dry, scaly, and easily penetrated. Harlequin ichthyosis, caused by ABCA12 mutations that block lipid loading of lamellar bodies, is the severe inherited form.

sections.title: Melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells

blocks.text: Three non-keratinocyte cells live in the epidermis, and each sits where its job requires. They are hard to tell apart on routine stains, so boards identify them by layer, origin, marker, and function.

Melanocytes arise from neural crest cells that migrate to the skin during embryonic life and settle in the stratum basale, roughly 1 for every 4 to 10 basal keratinocytes depending on region. They attach to the basement membrane but not to keratinocytes by desmosomes, so they look like pale clear cells on routine stains. Inside membrane-bound melanosomes, tyrosinase converts tyrosine to melanin. Melanocytes then extend dendrites between keratinocytes, and the keratinocytes take up the melanosome-filled tips. In each keratinocyte the melanin gathers over the sun-facing side of the nucleus as a cap that absorbs ultraviolet light before it reaches DNA.

blocks.title: Melanin synthesis and transfer
steps: Tyrosinase oxidizes tyrosine to DOPA, then DOPA to dopaquinone
Dopaquinone forms eumelanin, or pheomelanin when cysteine is added
Melanosomes mature and move out along melanocyte dendrites
Keratinocytes engulf dendrite tips containing melanosomes
Melanin forms a cap over each keratinocyte nucleus
blocks.caption: Alpha-MSH acting on the melanocortin 1 receptor favors brown-black eumelanin; ultraviolet light increases tyrosinase activity and transfer, producing a tan.

blocks.text: Skin color differs between people because of the number, size, melanin type, and breakdown rate of melanosomes, not because of melanocyte number, which is about the same in all skin colors. This explains two contrasting white-skin disorders. In oculocutaneous albinism type 1, melanocytes are present in normal numbers but tyrosinase is defective, so they cannot make pigment. In vitiligo, autoimmune destruction removes the melanocytes themselves.

Langerhans cells are dendritic antigen-presenting cells, mainly in the stratum spinosum, that are classically described as bone marrow derived. They express CD1a, langerin (CD207), and S-100, and on electron microscopy they contain rod-shaped Birbeck granules with a terminal bulb, the tennis-racket shape. They capture antigens and haptens, travel through dermal lymphatics to regional lymph nodes, and present them to naive T cells. This is the sensitization step of allergic contact dermatitis, a type IV reaction. Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a clonal proliferation of cells with the same markers.

Merkel cells sit in the stratum basale, joined to keratinocytes by desmosomes, and contain dense-core neurosecretory granules. Each contacts the expanded disc ending of a large myelinated sensory axon, forming a slowly adapting mechanoreceptor that signals sustained pressure, edges, and texture, so they are most numerous in fingertips and lips. Merkel cell carcinoma is an aggressive neuroendocrine skin cancer, often linked to Merkel cell polyomavirus.

sections.title: Desmosomes, hemidesmosomes, adherens junctions, and autoimmune blistering

blocks.text: The epidermis resists shearing because junctions tie the keratin network of every keratinocyte to its neighbors and to the basement membrane, turning the sheet into one mechanical unit. Remove any link and the tissue tears at that point, filling with fluid as a blister. The level of the tear identifies the protein that failed.

Desmosomes join keratinocyte to keratinocyte. Their calcium-dependent cadherins, desmogleins and desmocollins, bridge the space between cells, and a cytoplasmic plaque of plakoglobin, plakophilin, and desmoplakin anchors them to keratin. Desmoglein 3 is concentrated in the lower epidermis and in oral mucosa, while desmoglein 1 is concentrated in the upper epidermis and is scarce in mucosa. Adherens junctions also join neighboring cells, but through E-cadherin linked by catenins to actin; they organize the sheet and its signaling, and loss of E-cadherin lets carcinoma cells detach and invade. Hemidesmosomes join the basal cell to the basement membrane: integrin alpha6 beta4 binds laminin 332, the transmembrane protein BP180 (collagen XVII) reaches into the lamina lucida, and BP230 and plectin link these to keratins 5 and 14 inside the cell.

blocks.title: Keratinocyte junctions
rows: Pemphigus vulgaris and foliaceus; staphylococcal scalded skin
Loss of E-cadherin aids carcinoma invasion
BP180 (collagen XVII), BP230, integrin alpha6 beta4
Keratins 5 and 14, through plectin and BP230
blocks.caption: Desmosome problems split the epidermis from within; hemidesmosome problems lift the whole epidermis off the basement membrane.

blocks.text: In pemphigus vulgaris, IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3, often with desmoglein 1, cause acantholysis just above the basal layer. The basal cells stay attached by their hemidesmosomes and line the floor in a tombstone row. The roof is thin, so blisters are flaccid and rupture into erosions, oral lesions are nearly universal, the Nikolsky sign is positive, and direct immunofluorescence shows IgG between keratinocytes in a net-like pattern. In pemphigus foliaceus, antibodies only against desmoglein 1 split the epidermis just under the stratum corneum, producing crusted superficial erosions without mouth involvement. Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein 1 at the same level, causing bullous impetigo and scalded skin syndrome.

In bullous pemphigoid, IgG against BP180 and BP230 separates the entire epidermis from the basement membrane. The roof is full thickness, so blisters are tense, the Nikolsky sign is negative, mucosa is less often involved, and patients are usually older adults. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane, and biopsies contain many eosinophils.

blocks.title: Bullous pemphigoid pathogenesis
steps: IgG autoantibodies bind BP180 and BP230 at hemidesmosomes
Bound antibody activates complement along the basement membrane
Mast cells degranulate; eosinophils and neutrophils are recruited
Released proteases cleave the hemidesmosome attachments
Subepidermal split forms a tense, fluid-filled blister
blocks.caption: Complement and inflammatory cells, not antibody binding alone, cause most of the damage, which is why linear C3 accompanies IgG.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient whose antibodies target only desmoglein 1 have skin blisters but a normal mouth?
blocks.explain: Oral mucosa contains abundant desmoglein 3 and little desmoglein 1, so intact desmoglein 3 keeps mucosal cells attached. In skin, the upper epidermis relies mainly on desmoglein 1, so it splits there. When antibodies to desmoglein 3 are added, the mucosa fails as well, as in pemphigus vulgaris.
blocks.check: The distribution of desmogleins 1 and 3 and the pemphigus paragraph.

sections.title: The dermal-epidermal junction and the level of the split

blocks.text: Below the basal keratinocyte lies the basement membrane zone, which electron microscopy resolves into three layers. The lamina lucida is a pale band crossed by anchoring filaments of laminin 332 and the extracellular part of collagen XVII, which tie hemidesmosomes downward. The lamina densa is a sheet of type IV collagen with nidogen and perlecan, the same network found in all basement membranes. Below it, anchoring fibrils of type VII collagen loop from the lamina densa into the papillary dermis and trap its type I and III collagen fibers.

Each component is a link in a chain, and the chain breaks at the weakest link. A blister therefore forms just above the structure that still holds, and its floor and roof tell you the level. Inherited defects (epidermolysis bullosa) and autoantibodies follow the same map.

blocks.title: Split level by failed component
rows: Laminin 332, collagen XVII, integrin alpha6 beta4
Usually without scarring; atrophy possible in junctional forms
blocks.caption: Deeper splits tear the papillary dermis, so they heal with scarring; splits above the lamina densa leave the basement membrane on the floor.

blocks.text: Depth explains the clinical picture. Splits at or above the lamina densa leave an intact basement membrane on which keratinocytes can migrate, so they usually heal without scars. Splits below it disrupt the papillary dermis, so they heal with scarring and milia (small keratin cysts), and the recessive form of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa produces fused fingers and a high risk of squamous cell carcinoma in chronic wounds. Integrin alpha6 beta4 defects cause junctional disease with pyloric atresia because the same integrin anchors gut epithelium. Antibodies to type IV collagen do not blister the skin: anti-glomerular basement membrane disease targets the alpha3 chain, which is present in kidney and lung basement membranes but not in the epidermal lamina densa.

blocks.title: Using the split level to separate two lookalike diseases
blocks.text: Two adults have tense subepidermal blisters with linear IgG along the basement membrane. One heals cleanly; the other heals with scars and milia on the hands and elbows. Scarring means a split below the lamina densa, so the second patient's antibodies target type VII collagen (epidermolysis bullosa acquisita), not BP180 or BP230. The lab can confirm this with salt-split skin: incubating normal skin in 1 M sodium chloride separates it through the lamina lucida. Bullous pemphigoid antibodies bind the roof (the hemidesmosome side), while antibodies to type VII collagen bind the floor (the dermal side).

sections.title: Papillary dermis, reticular dermis, and hypodermis

blocks.text: The dermis is the mesoderm-derived connective tissue that gives skin its strength, recoil, blood supply, and most of its sensation. It has two layers built for different loads, and beneath it the hypodermis (subcutis) joins skin to deeper fascia.

The papillary dermis is a thin layer of loose connective tissue with fine type III and type I collagen, thin elastic fibers, and many fibroblasts, mast cells, and macrophages. It rises into dermal papillae that interlock with the downward epidermal ridges (rete ridges), which enlarges the contact surface and resists shear. Capillary loops in each papilla nourish the avascular epidermis by diffusion, and in hairless (glabrous) skin many papillae hold a Meissner corpuscle.

The reticular dermis is much thicker dense irregular connective tissue. Coarse bundles of type I collagen give tensile strength, coarse elastic fibers give recoil, and the bases of hair follicles and glands sit here. Collagen bundles run in preferred directions that form the skin tension (cleavage) lines, so an incision along them gapes less and leaves a finer scar. The hypodermis is not part of the skin proper; it is loose connective tissue and fat lobules divided by fibrous septa that insulate, store energy, cushion, and carry the larger vessels and nerves.

Meissner corpuscles in glabrous skin; free nerve endings
Dense irregular; coarse type I collagen, coarse elastic fibers
Deep plexus at the dermis-hypodermis border

Loose tissue with fat lobules and fibrous septa
Pacinian corpuscles; deep coils of some sweat glands
blocks.caption: Two horizontal vascular plexuses, connected by vertical vessels, supply the dermis; the epidermis itself has no vessels.

blocks.text: Arteriovenous anastomoses, most numerous in the fingers, toes, and ears, let sympathetic nerves divert blood toward or away from the surface plexus, which is a major route of heat loss. Receptor depth follows function. Meissner corpuscles sit just under the epidermis and adapt quickly, signaling light touch and low-frequency flutter. Pacinian corpuscles lie deep, and their onion-like capsule filters out steady pressure so they respond only to rapid change and high-frequency vibration. Free nerve endings of thin A delta and C fibers extend into the epidermis and signal pain, temperature, and itch.

blocks.title: Cutaneous receptors
blocks.caption: Superficial receptors give fine spatial detail; deep receptors sense vibration transmitted through tissue.

blocks.text: Each layer has its own disorders. Chronic sun exposure degrades papillary dermal collagen and deposits abnormal elastic material (solar elastosis), producing wrinkles. Inherited collagen defects such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome make the dermis hyperextensible and fragile. Inflammation centered in the hypodermal septa, as in erythema nodosum, produces tender nodules rather than surface change.

Skin glands are separated by three questions: where they open, how they release product, and what controls them. Eccrine glands open directly onto the surface; apocrine and sebaceous glands usually open into hair follicles, so neither is found on the palms and soles.

blocks.title: Skin glands compared
rows: Nearly all skin, densest on palms, soles, forehead; opens on surface
Sympathetic cholinergic fibers on muscarinic (M3) receptors
Hyperhidrosis; salty sweat in cystic fibrosis
Axilla, areola, anogenital skin; opens into follicle
Viscous, odorless until skin bacteria act on it
All hair-bearing skin; opens into follicle; none on palms and soles
blocks.caption: Modified apocrine glands include ceruminous glands of the ear canal and glands of Moll in the eyelid; meibomian glands are modified sebaceous glands that open directly on the lid margin.

blocks.text: Eccrine glands are the main tool of evaporative cooling. A coiled secretory portion in the deep dermis makes a fluid close to plasma in sodium and chloride, and the duct then reabsorbs sodium through ENaC and chloride through CFTR, so normal sweat reaching the surface is hypotonic. In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR blocks ductal chloride reabsorption, which is why sweat chloride is high (about 60 mmol/L or more supports the diagnosis). These glands break the usual sympathetic rule: postganglionic sympathetic fibers release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors. Hyperhidrosis is sweating beyond thermal need; the primary focal form affects palms, soles, and axillae through excess sympathetic drive to normal glands, while secondary generalized forms follow fever, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, or pheochromocytoma.

Apocrine glands have a wide lumen and empty into the follicle above the sebaceous duct. They enlarge at puberty and respond mainly to adrenergic stimulation such as emotional stress. Sebaceous glands release sebum (triglycerides, wax esters, squalene) by holocrine secretion: basal cells divide, fill with lipid, die, and break apart. Androgens, largely converted to dihydrotestosterone within the gland, enlarge sebaceous glands and increase output, which explains their activity at birth (maternal hormones) and puberty.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of acne
steps: Androgens enlarge sebaceous glands and increase sebum output
Abnormal keratinization plugs the follicle, forming a microcomedo
Cutibacterium acnes multiplies in the lipid-rich, low-oxygen plug
Bacterial lipases and TLR2 signaling trigger inflammation
Follicle wall ruptures into dermis, forming papules, pustules, nodules
blocks.caption: Acne is a disease of the pilosebaceous unit, so it spares the palms and soles, which have no sebaceous glands.

blocks.predict: A person taking a drug with strong antimuscarinic action exercises in hot weather. What happens to sweating and body temperature?
blocks.explain: Eccrine glands are driven by acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors even though the fibers are sympathetic, so sweating stops. Without evaporative cooling, heat is retained and core temperature rises, and the skin is hot, dry, and flushed. Apocrine secretion, which is mainly adrenergic, is little affected and contributes almost nothing to cooling.

sections.title: Hair follicle, hair cycle, and nail unit

blocks.text: A hair follicle is a downgrowth of epidermis into the dermis. Its deepest part, the bulb, holds matrix cells that divide rapidly around the dermal papilla, a cluster of specialized fibroblasts and capillaries whose signals start growth and set hair size. Matrix cells form the hair shaft and the inner root sheath, and bulb melanocytes color the shaft. The outer root sheath is continuous with the epidermis. Where the arrector pili muscle inserts, the outer root sheath forms the bulge, which holds multipotent stem cells that rebuild the lower follicle at each new cycle and help repair the epidermis after wounds.

The arrector pili is smooth muscle running from the bulge to the papillary dermis. Sympathetic alpha1-adrenergic stimulation contracts it, raising the hair and pressing on the sebaceous gland. Diseases that destroy the bulge cause scarring, permanent alopecia, while telogen effluvium, alopecia areata, and androgenetic alopecia spare the bulge and allow regrowth.

blocks.title: The scalp hair cycle
rows: Matrix cells divide and the shaft lengthens; duration sets maximum length
Matrix cells undergo apoptosis; lower follicle regresses toward the bulge
Club hair rests, then is shed as a new anagen hair grows beneath it
blocks.caption: Shedding about 50 to 100 scalp hairs a day is normal because follicles cycle out of step with each other.

blocks.title: Telogen effluvium
steps: Stressor: high fever, childbirth, surgery, severe illness, crash diet
Many anagen follicles enter catagen early and together
Follicles rest in telogen for about 3 months
New anagen hairs push out the club hairs
Diffuse shedding begins 2 to 3 months after the stressor
blocks.caption: The bulge is spared, so the loss is nonscarring and hair regrows over months once the stressor is gone.

blocks.title: Using timing to name the hair loss
blocks.text: A woman notices diffuse shedding of whole hairs with small white bulbs 3 months after delivering a baby. Another patient loses most of her scalp hair 2 weeks after starting chemotherapy. Work from the cycle. Club hairs that fall about 3 months after a stressor are telogen hairs, so the first patient has telogen effluvium. Chemotherapy halts mitosis in matrix cells of growing anagen follicles, so the shaft narrows and breaks within days to weeks, which is anagen effluvium. The delay is the length of telogen; the speed is the dependence of anagen on dividing cells.

The nail plate is hard keratin made by the nail matrix, which lies under the proximal nail fold; the pale lunula is the visible distal edge of the matrix. The plate slides forward over the nail bed, whose vascular dermis makes the nail look pink, and its free edge overhangs the hyponychium. The cuticle, made by the proximal fold (eponychium), seals the plate, and lateral folds frame its sides. Fingernails grow about 3 mm per month and toenails about 1 mm per month. Matrix injury causes permanent deformity, and a brief arrest of matrix growth during severe illness leaves a transverse groove (Beau line), the nail counterpart of telogen effluvium.

An ingrown nail usually involves the great toe. When the lateral edge of the plate is cut short and curved, or compressed by tight footwear, it grows into the soft tissue of the lateral nail fold. The plate then acts as a foreign body, provoking inflammation, granulation tissue, and often bacterial infection of the fold (paronychia).
Dermatopathology terms name the abnormal layer or process, so each points to a mechanism: a layer too thick, a maturation step skipped, or cell connections failing.

blocks.title: Six core terms
rows: More corneocytes made, or normal ones shed too slowly
Nuclei retained in the stratum corneum
Maturation so fast that nuclei are not destroyed
Fluid between keratinocytes that remain attached
Desmosome failure, usually from anti-desmoglein antibodies
Single keratinocytes keratinize early and abnormally
Actinic keratosis, squamous cell carcinoma, Darier disease
blocks.caption: Two pairs are often confused: hyperkeratosis (corneum) versus acanthosis (spinosum), and spongiosis (edema, cells attached) versus acantholysis (cells detached).

blocks.text: Psoriasis shows how several terms arise from one mechanism. Dendritic cells release IL-23, which sustains Th17 cells, and their IL-17 and IL-22 drive keratinocyte proliferation. Transit through the epidermis falls from about 4 weeks to a few days, so the spinous layer thickens with long, regular rete ridges (acanthosis), cells reach the surface without passing through a normal granular layer, and nuclei are retained (parakeratosis) in a thick scale. Neutrophils collect in the corneum as Munro microabscesses. Capillaries in the papillae dilate while the epidermis over them thins, so lifting a scale causes pinpoint bleeding (the Auspitz sign).

Eczematous dermatitis is the prototype of spongiosis. Inflammation, from Th2 responses in atopic dermatitis or hapten-specific T cells in allergic contact dermatitis, lets fluid enter the epidermis and push keratinocytes apart while their desmosomes hold, so the junctions appear prominent. Severe spongiosis forms small intraepidermal vesicles, and chronic scratching adds acanthosis and hyperkeratosis (lichenification). Acantholysis differs because adhesion itself is lost: in pemphigus, detached keratinocytes round up and float freely in the blister. Dyskeratosis signals disordered maturation of individual cells and, with atypia, is a feature of dysplasia and squamous cell carcinoma, where keratin pearls form.

integration.text: Skin structure ties the Part I disciplines together through one idea: each level is held by specific proteins, and failure of a protein produces a predictable lesion. Embryology supplies the cells, with ectoderm forming keratinocytes, neural crest forming melanocytes, mesoderm forming the dermis, and hematopoietic precursors supplying Langerhans cells. Biochemistry and genetics explain inherited fragility (keratins, laminin 332, collagens XVII and VII), barrier failure (filaggrin), and pigment disorders (tyrosinase). Immunology explains the acquired forms, with type II autoantibodies against desmogleins and hemidesmosome proteins and type IV sensitization through Langerhans cells. Microbiology appears where bacterial toxins cleave desmoglein 1 and where Cutibacterium acnes inflames a plugged follicle.

Pathology uses the same map in reverse. A biopsy reports a split level and a histologic term, and immunofluorescence reports the pattern of antibody, and from these the target protein can be inferred. The limits are real: clinical blister type overlaps, early lesions may lack the classic picture, and some diseases involve more than one antigen, so split level, immunofluorescence, and the clinical setting are read together rather than relying on any single finding.

summary: Keratinocytes mature from basale to corneum over about 4 weeks, switching from keratins 5 and 14 to 1 and 10; stratum lucidum appears only in thick skin of the palms and soles.
The barrier forms in the granulosum: filaggrin bundles keratin, lamellar bodies secrete lipid, and transglutaminase builds the cornified envelope.
Melanocytes (neural crest, basal layer) transfer melanosomes to keratinocytes; skin color reflects melanosome activity, not melanocyte number.
Langerhans cells (CD1a, langerin, Birbeck granules) carry antigen to lymph nodes; Merkel cells are slowly adapting touch receptors in the basal layer.

Anti-desmoglein antibodies split the epidermis from within (pemphigus, flaccid blisters, Nikolsky positive); anti-BP180 and BP230 antibodies lift it off the basement membrane (bullous pemphigoid, tense blisters).
Split level predicts the protein: keratin 5 or 14 within basal cells, laminin 332 or collagen XVII in the lamina lucida, type VII collagen below the lamina densa with scarring and milia.
The papillary dermis is loose with capillary loops and Meissner corpuscles; the reticular dermis is dense type I collagen; Pacinian corpuscles lie deep.
Eccrine glands are sympathetic but muscarinic and open on the surface; apocrine and sebaceous glands open into follicles, and androgen-driven sebum underlies acne.
Telogen effluvium appears about 2 to 3 months after a stressor because telogen lasts about 3 months; bulge destruction causes permanent, scarring alopecia.
Hyperkeratosis and acanthosis describe thick corneum and spinosum; parakeratosis means retained nuclei; spongiosis is edema with cells attached, acantholysis is cells detached.

verify: Langerhans cells are taught as bone marrow derived, but current evidence shows they are seeded before birth from yolk sac and fetal liver precursors and are replaced by bone marrow monocytes after inflammation; confirm which origin NABNE expects.
The embryonic origin of Merkel cells was long given as neural crest, but lineage studies support an epidermal (keratinocyte lineage) origin; the table refers here rather than stating one.
Epidermal turnover time is quoted from about 28 to 45 days, and the melanocyte to basal cell ratio from about 1 to 4 up to 1 to 10; values here are approximate.
Hair cycle durations and the percentage of scalp hairs in each phase vary between sources (anagen 2 to 7 years, telogen 10 to 15%).
The sweat chloride cutoff of about 60 mmol/L follows current cystic fibrosis diagnostic consensus; confirm the value NABNE uses.
Whether apocrine glands secrete by true decapitation (apocrine) or largely merocrine release is debated; the chapter does not rely on the mechanism of release.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Nikolsky, Auspitz, Munro, Beau, Birbeck, Meissner, Pacinian, Merkel, and Ruffini, or only descriptive terms.
